q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Anne Boleyn was English. She and Henry had one daughter, Elizabeth. Anne was unpopular in the country and was accused of taking lovers. She was executed at the Tower of London. Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess.
o: Anne Boleyn was executed at the Tower of London
Catherine of Aragon was executed at the Tower of London

q.t: Which of Henry VIII's wives gave him the son he wanted?
q.e: Jane Seymour: Henry married Jane after Anne's execution. She gave Henry the son he wanted, Edward, but she died shortly after the birth.

q.t: Which TWO of Henry VIII's wives were executed?
q.e: Anne Boleyn was accused of taking lovers and was executed at the Tower of London. Catherine Howard was a cousin of Anne Boleyn. She was also accused of taking lovers and executed.

q.t: Why did Henry VIII establish the Church of England?
q.e: To divorce his first wife, Henry needed the approval of the Pope. When the Pope refused, Henry established the Church of England. In this new Church, the king, not the Pope, would have the power to appoint bishops.
o: The Pope refused to approve his divorce
Parliament ordered him to do so
He wished to join the Reformation in Scotland
He wanted to translate the Bible into English

q.t: During whose reign was the Book of Common Prayer written?
q.e: Henry VIII was succeeded by his son Edward VI, who was strongly Protestant. During his reign, the Book of Common Prayer was written to be used in the Church of England. Edward died at the age of 15.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Mary I was a devout Catholic who persecuted Protestants and became known as 'Bloody Mary'.
q.e: Mary was a devout Catholic and persecuted Protestants, and for this reason she became known as 'Bloody Mary'. Mary also died after a short reign and the next monarch was her half-sister Elizabeth.

q.t: In 1588 the English defeated the Spanish Armada. Why had it been sent?
q.e: Elizabeth became one of the most popular monarchs in English history, particularly after 1588, when the English defeated the Spanish Armada, a large fleet of ships, which had been sent by Spain to conquer England and restore Catholicism.
o: To conquer England and restore Catholicism
To support Mary, Queen of Scots in Scotland
To colonise the eastern coast of America

q.t: For how long did Elizabeth I keep Mary, Queen of Scots a prisoner?
q.e: Mary was Elizabeth I's cousin and hoped that Elizabeth might help her, but Elizabeth suspected Mary of wanting to take over the English throne, and kept her a prisoner for 20 years. Mary was eventually executed.

q.t: How old was Mary, Queen of Scots when she became queen of Scotland?
q.e: The queen of Scotland, Mary Stuart, often now called 'Mary, Queen of Scots', was a Catholic. She was only a week old when her father died and she became queen. Much of her childhood was spent in France.
o: She was only a week old

q.t: Which ship was one of the first to sail right around the world?
q.e: Sir Francis Drake, one of the commanders in the defeat of the Spanish Armada, was one of the founders of England's naval tradition. His ship, the Golden Hind, was one of the first to sail right around, or circumnavigate, the world.

q.t: Which TWO lines below are from plays by William Shakespeare, according to the handbook?
q.e: Lines from Shakespeare's plays and poems which are often still quoted include: Once more unto the breach from Henry V, To be or not to be from Hamlet, A rose by any other name from Romeo and Juliet, and All the world's a stage from As You Like It.
o: To be or not to be
I wander'd lonely as a cloud
She walks in beauty, like the night

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The Globe Theatre in London is the original theatre in which Shakespeare's plays were first performed.
q.e: Many people regard Shakespeare as the greatest playwright of all time. The Globe Theatre in London is a modern copy of the theatres in which his plays were first performed.

q.t: Which national flower is associated with Wales?
q.e: The countries that make up the UK all have flowers which are particularly associated with them: England the rose, Scotland the thistle, Wales the daffodil, and Northern Ireland the shamrock.

q.t: Which traditional food is a sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, suet, onions and oatmeal?
q.e: Scotland: haggis, a sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, suet, onions and oatmeal. Northern Ireland has the Ulster fry and Wales has Welsh cakes.

q.t: Which TWO items are part of the traditional Ulster fry?
q.e: Northern Ireland: Ulster fry, a fried meal with bacon, eggs, sausage, black pudding, white pudding, tomatoes, mushrooms, soda bread and potato bread.

q.t: In which year were films first shown publicly in the UK?
q.e: Films were first shown publicly in the UK in 1896 and film screenings very quickly became popular. From the beginning, film makers became famous for clever special effects.

q.t: For which character did Sir Charles Chaplin become famous in silent movies?
q.e: From the early days of the cinema, British actors have worked in both the UK and USA. Sir Charles (Charlie) Chaplin became famous in silent movies for his tramp character and was one of many British actors to make a career in Hollywood.

q.t: How many Oscars has Nick Park won, and for what?
q.e: Britain continues to be particularly strong in special effects and animation. One example is the work of Nick Park, who has won four Oscars for his animated films, including three for films featuring Wallace and Gromit.
o: Four Oscars for his animated films
Four Oscars for directing James Bond films

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Criminal law relates to crimes, which are usually investigated by the police or another authority such as a council, and which are punished by the courts. Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups.
o: Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups
Criminal law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups

q.t: Which TWO of these are given as examples of civil law?
q.e: Examples of civil laws are housing law, including disputes between landlords and tenants; consumer rights, such as a dispute about faulty goods or services; employment law; and debt.
o: A dispute about faulty goods or services

q.t: What are the three duties of the police, according to the handbook?
q.e: The job of the police in the UK is to protect life and property, prevent disturbances, also known as keeping the peace, and prevent and detect crime.
o: Protect life and property, keep the peace, and prevent and detect crime
Collect taxes, keep the peace, and run the courts
Protect life and property, set sentences, and run prisons
Investigate crime, pass laws, and appoint judges

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
It is a criminal offence to carry a weapon of any kind, even if it is for self-defence.
q.e: Carrying a weapon: it is a criminal offence to carry a weapon of any kind, even if it is for self-defence. This includes a gun, a knife or anything that is made or adapted to cause injury.

q.t: Who appoints the Chief Constable in England and Wales?
q.e: Police and Crime Commissioners are directly elected individuals who are responsible for the delivery of an efficient and effective police force. PCCs set local police priorities and the local policing budget. They also appoint the Chief Constable.

q.t: Which of these are residents of the UK expected to do, according to the handbook?
q.e: If you wish to be a permanent resident or citizen of the UK, you should respect and obey the law, respect the rights of others including their right to their own opinions, treat others with fairness, look after yourself and your family, and look after the area in which you live and the environment.
o: Look after the area in which they live and the environment
Attend a place of worship weekly
